# Data Analytics {#sec-data-analytics}

## Spatial Unit Analysis

Every trip carries its location in three encodings, separately for pickup
and dropoff: a community area (the 77 official Chicago community areas), a tract (~800 tracts),
and a latitude/longitude coordinate pair. The data providers already document two caveats.
The census tract may be blank for privacy reasons, and the latitude/longitude is the centroid
of the census tract, or the centroid of the community area when the tract is suppressed [@chicago_privacy_story].
The coordinate is therefore not a raw GPS fix but a centroid whose true resolution depends
on whether the tract survived anonymisation. In this section, we outline the pyhsical distribution of the coordinates
and therfore of the trips, in order to argue for our unit of analysis for demand prediction.

First we conduct a short missingness and consistency check, which gives us three key findings.
First, the census tract is missing for roughly 55 % of trips, while
the community area is essentially complete (missing only about 7 % of dropoffs),
so location is almost always known at community-area resolution but only sometimes
at tract resolution. Second, the encodings nest cleanly: every coordinate maps to
exactly one community area and one census tract, and every tract to exactly one community
area. Third, because the coordinate is a centroid we can recover which level it
represents per trip, and the split is almost even, with about 45 % of trips
resolved at census-tract level and 55 % only at community-area level.

This pattern is visible geographically. Scattering every coordinate over the
community areas (@fig-coords-community) and over the census tracts
(@fig-coords-tract) shows that in the centre of the city the points sit at
census-tract centroids, resolving fine detail, whereas on the outskirts they
collapse onto a sparser set of community-area centroids, exactly the pattern
the privacy suppression would produce.

An alternative to the administrative units is a regular H3 hexagon grid,
which gives equal-area cells independent of the political boundaries.
Overlaying the trip endpoints on H3 grids at four resolutions, with the community-area boundaries added for reference
(@fig-hex-community), shows that because the coordinates are a limited set
of centroids rather than continuous GPS points, a large share of the
hexagons contain no points at all, especially at the finer resolutions
and towards the city edge. A raw hexagon binning of the coordinates
would therefore be dominated by empty cells.

To bridge the two tilings we tested areal interpolation: count trip
endpoints per community area, then distribute each area's count onto the
hexagons in proportion to their geometric overlap. This conserves essentially
all of the endpoints (@fig-areal-weighted), but
it smooths the data, because trips are assumed uniform within each community
area, so the outskirts become artificially homogeneous and the real
concentration of activity is blurred.

Comparing the areal-weighted hexagons against the raw community-area counts
(@fig-trips-community) makes the trade-off concrete. The areal weighting
smoothes the trips out, most notably in the airport area in the north west.
Therfore, the community-area choropleth is a direct, real-world measure of activity that introduces no
modelling assumption. In addition, the census-tract choropleth (@fig-trips-tract)
offers finer detail but confirms that the outskirts are barely covered,
because those trips only ever carried a community-area location, similarly to finer
hexagon representation without areal weighting. We therefore
adopt the community area as the primary spatial unit for the descriptive
analysis, as it is complete, internally consistent with the finer encodings,
and free of both the smoothing artefacts of areal weighting and the empty-cell
sparsity of a raw hexagon grid. Where finer resolution is genuinely available
and useful, the census tract remains a secondary view. In terms of fleet managmenet
the community area demand is a valuable metric to orchestrate the amount of taxis needed
in a certain area, with predictions being accurate enough and within a reasonably sized area
for taxis to operate in.

## Spatial and temporal demand patterns {#sec-spatial-temporal-demand-patterns}

Taking the community area as our main spatial unit, we now characterise how demand
varies across space and time for this unit. All maps in this part are drawn as paired
choropleths, with pickups on the left and dropoffs on the right, so in addition to the
volume, the direction of demand is visible.

First, we can see how demand concentrates over the community areas with espacially high
trip volumes at O'Hare International Airport in the far north-west and the downtown
lakefront cluster (@fig-trips-community). The remainder of the city is close to empty by comparison.
The paired map (@fig-demand-spatial) also exposes a
asymmetry at O'Hare airport, being near-maximal as a source of pickups but
only moderate as a dropoff destination, suggesting that arriving air passengers take taxis away
from the terminal far more often than departing ones are dropped there. Downtown,
by contrast, is roughly symmetric, both generating and attracting trips. Notably,
Midway, the city's second airport to the south-west, barely registers, so the
airport signal in this dataset is essentially an O'Hare signal. For a fleet
operator this implies supply must be pre-positioned at O'Hare and downtown, and
that vehicles will tend to accumulate downtown-bound out of the airport and need
active rebalancing back. The census-tract equivalent (@fig-demand-spatial-tract)
resolves both poles into individual tracts and reproduces the same O'Hare
asymmetry, with the suppressed periphery emptier still, consistent with the
coverage gap described above.

A hotspot analysis quantifies this picture. Fitting a Gaussian Mixture Model
(GMM) to the pickup and dropoff coordinates, with the number of components
chosen by AIC (K = 14 pickups, K = 15 dropoffs) and cross-checked against a
kernel density estimate, decomposes demand into named, ranked components
(@fig-kde-hotspots, @fig-gmm-hotspots, @tbl-hotspot-ranking). Near North Side
(22.2 % of pickups) and the Loop (21.2 %) are the two largest pickup
components, while the Loop alone accounts for 26.1 % of dropoffs. O'Hare
splits into two adjacent components jointly holding 21.2 % of pickups but
only 4.7 % of dropoffs, giving the pickup-heavy airport asymmetry a concrete
figure. Because the GMM is a soft-clustering model, it also shows where this
structure blurs: 18.1 % of pickup points and 22.5 % of dropoff points cannot
be assigned to a single hotspot with more than 80 % certainty, so demand at
basin boundaries, e.g. between the Loop and Near North Side, is genuinely
shared rather than attributable to one pole, a nuance a hard fleet-zoning
rule would miss.

Understanding the temporal distrubution, several things are noteworthy.
Collapsing the spatial dimension and keeping time
(@fig-hourly-demand) reveals a sharp diurnal cycle: demand is negligible
overnight, ramps up steeply from around 05:00, and peaks at 17:00 before
declining into the night. Pickup and dropoff curves almost coincide; the small
lead–lag between them is merely trip duration shifting dropoffs into slightly
later hours, not a strong directional commuting effect. The 8-hour-block maps
(@fig-block-demand) place this in space: the overnight block (00:00–07:59) is
near-empty everywhere, while the midday and most of all the evening block
concentrate activity on the O'Hare pickup pole and the downtown core. Across the
week (@fig-dow-demand) weekdays are near-identical, but Saturday softens the
O'Hare (airport and business-travel) pole while downtown activity holds up,
consistent with a shift from business to leisure travel. Sunday then recovers the
airport component as travellers return. Seasonally (@fig-month-demand) the
spatial structure is invariant, but overall volume varies over the year.
Collapsing space and keeping time, as for the hourly view, quantifies this
precisely: the monthly total (@fig-monthly-demand) confirms December as the
year's low nt. Finally, the demand geography is remarkably 
robust on public holidays (@fig-holiday-demand): the airport and downtown poles
persist across all four holiday flags, so atypical calendar days rescale demand
rather than relocating it. All of these patterns hold essentially unchanged at
census-tract resolution (@fig-hourly-demand-tract, @fig-block-demand-tract,
@fig-dow-demand-tract, @fig-month-demand-tract,
@fig-holiday-demand-tract): the hourly and monthly curves are identical, since
collapsing the spatial dimension erases any difference between the two units,
while the block, weekday, monthly and holiday maps merely resolve the same two
poles into finer tracts, with the suppressed periphery going emptier still.

Averaging trip attributes per area separates the
features into two clean groups. The weather variables (temperature, precipitation,
humidity, wind, snow) are essentially uniform across the city, weather is a
temporal signal, not a spatial one, and enters the predictive models on the
time axis rather than as a per-area feature. The trip-economics variables, in
contrast, show a strong spatial gradient (@fig-feature-gradient). Mean fare and
mean trip distance rise toward O'Hare and the outer periphery, while mean speed
falls in the congested core. In short, centrality and trip value move in opposite
directions with short, cheap, slow trips in downtown versus long, expensive, fast trips
from the edges and the airport. For an electric fleet this gradient is doubly
relevant as peripheral and airport trips are not only higher-revenue but also
higher-energy comsuming, with direct implications for vehicle range and charging strategy.
The same gradient holds at census-tract resolution (@fig-feature-gradient-tract),
confirming it is not an artefact of community-area aggregation. The full
19-feature grid at both resolutions, and the day-of-week, block, month and
holiday maps, are provided in Appendix -@sec-appendix.

Finally, we outline the effect of points of interest (POI) on the demand.
The urban-mobility literature treats POI as a strong driver
of where taxi demand arises. We test whether that holds for Chicago before
committing to POI as a modelling input. For each of the 77 community areas we
sum the eight POI categories (healthcare, education, amenity, leisure, shops,
public services, tourism, nature) into a single density measure and plot it
against taxi activity, measured as the number of trip endpoints (pickup plus
dropoff) that fall within the area.

@fig-poi-demand shows a strong positive association on a log-log scale: areas
richer in points of interest handle markedly more taxi trips, with the three
busiest areas, the Near North Side, the Loop and O'Hare, sitting in the
top-right corner. The rank correlation is high (Spearman $\rho = 0.79$), and the
log-log Pearson correlation is even higher ($r = 0.85$), confirming that the
relationship is close to a straight power law across all 77 areas rather than
being driven by a few downtown outliers. In plain terms, roughly each tenfold
increase in POI count comes with a comparable rise in taxi activity. The main
exception is O'Hare, which generates far more trips than its moderate on-site POI
count alone would predict, an airport effect rather than a neighbourhood-amenity
effect, while a cluster of POI-sparse outer areas at the lower-left sustains only
light, corridor-driven traffic.

The conclusion is twofold. Descriptively, POI density offers an intuitive,
non-technical explanation for the demand hot spots a fleet operator would care
about. Practically, this correlation is what justifies carrying POI density
forward as an engineered feature in the predictive models, rather than
leaving it as a standalone map. The full per-category maps, at both census-tract
and community-area resolution, are provided in Appendix -@sec-appendix (@fig-poi-tract,
@fig-poi-community).
